documents.name: solar-power.pdf
pages: Photovoltaic cells are made from silicon wafers. When photons strike the wafer they knock electrons loose, creating a direct current. A typical residential panel holds sixty cells wired in series and converts roughly twenty percent of sunlight into electricity. Efficiency drops as cell temperature rises, so panels perform best on cool, clear days.

An inverter converts the direct current from panels into alternating current that matches the grid frequency. String inverters serve a whole row of panels, while microinverters sit behind each panel and keep the rest of the array running if one panel is shaded. Grid-tied systems must shut down automatically during an outage so that utility workers are not endangered by power flowing back into the lines.

Home batteries store surplus solar energy for the evening. Lithium iron phosphate cells are popular because they tolerate many charge cycles and are less prone to overheating. A typical household battery holds between ten and fifteen kilowatt hours, enough to cover an evening of cooking, lighting and television but not a full day of heating.

Solar arrays need little maintenance. Rain washes away most dust, though bird droppings and fallen leaves should be cleared by hand. Output declines by about half a percent each year as the silicon degrades, and most manufacturers guarantee eighty percent of original output after twenty five years. Inverters usually fail first and are replaced after ten to fifteen years.

documents.name: wind-power.pdf
pages: Turbine blades work like aeroplane wings. Air flowing over the curved surface creates lift that turns the rotor. Pitch control twists each blade to catch more or less wind, and in storms the blades are feathered to stop the rotor. Most large turbines begin generating at about three metres per second and shut down above twenty five metres per second to avoid damage.

Offshore wind farms sit on monopile foundations driven into the seabed in shallow water, or on floating platforms anchored by cables in deep water. Wind at sea is stronger and steadier than on land, which raises output, but salt water corrosion and installation by specialised vessels make the turbines far more expensive to build and service.

Wind farms connect to the grid through transformers that step up the voltage for long distance transmission. When the grid cannot absorb all the power on a windy day, operators order curtailment, paying wind farms to switch off. Better transmission lines and storage reduce curtailment and make wind output easier to balance against demand.

Gearboxes are the most failure prone part of a wind turbine, followed by the generator bearings. Technicians climb the tower twice a year to inspect blades for cracks and lightning damage, and sensors in the nacelle monitor vibration to predict faults before they cause costly downtime. Direct drive generators remove the gearbox entirely but need expensive permanent magnets.

documents.name: home-heating.pdf
pages: A heat pump moves heat rather than creating it. Refrigerant absorbs warmth from outside air or the ground, is compressed to raise its temperature, and releases that heat inside the house. For every unit of electricity used, a good heat pump delivers three to four units of heat, a ratio known as the coefficient of performance. Performance falls in very cold weather.

Insulation slows the escape of heat through the loft, walls and floor. Loft insulation is the cheapest upgrade and can cut heating bills by around fifteen percent. Cavity wall filling and double glazing follow, while draught proofing around doors and windows costs little. A well insulated home also lets a smaller, cheaper heating system do the job.

Condensing gas boilers capture heat from exhaust gases that older boilers wasted, reaching efficiencies above ninety percent. A combi boiler heats water on demand and removes the need for a storage tank, but its flow rate drops when two taps run at once. Boilers should be serviced annually, and carbon monoxide alarms must be fitted nearby.

Smart thermostats learn when the household is home and lower the temperature while everyone is out. Zoned radiator valves let each room be heated to its own schedule. Setting the thermostat one degree lower saves roughly ten percent on heating costs. Weather compensation adjusts boiler flow temperature automatically as the outside temperature changes.

documents.name: solar-thermal.pdf
pages: Solar thermal collectors heat water directly instead of making electricity. Flat plate collectors on the roof pass fluid through a dark absorber plate, and a pump carries the warmed fluid to a hot water cylinder. A typical household system supplies about sixty percent of annual hot water, with a gas boiler or immersion heater covering the rest in winter.

Evacuated tube collectors hold each pipe inside a glass vacuum tube that cuts heat loss, so they work better in cold, cloudy weather than flat plates. They cost more per panel and snow can lie on them for days because little heat escapes to melt it. Overheating in summer is prevented by a controller that stops the pump.

Solar thermal systems need an annual check of the glycol antifreeze in the pipework, which degrades after about five years and must be replaced. The pump and controller are the usual failure points. Unlike photovoltaic panels, a thermal collector keeps working during a power cut only if the pump has a battery backup.

documents.name: battery-storage.pdf
pages: Lead acid batteries were the first choice for off grid cabins but allow only fifty percent depth of discharge before wear sets in. They last around five years and need ventilation because they release hydrogen while charging. Their low price per kilowatt hour still suits seasonal holiday homes used a few weeks each summer.

Sodium ion batteries use cheap abundant sodium instead of lithium and tolerate freezing temperatures well. Their energy density is lower, so a sodium unit takes more wall space for the same capacity. Several manufacturers began selling them for home storage after lithium prices spiked, though cycle life is still being proven.

Battery capacity is quoted in kilowatt hours, but usable capacity is lower because the battery management system reserves a safety margin. A ten kilowatt hour unit may offer only nine usable. Round trip efficiency, the share of stored energy you get back, is typically ninety percent for lithium and eighty percent for lead acid.

documents.name: heat-pump-installer.pdf
pages: Installers size a heat pump by calculating the heat loss of each room, measured in watts. An oversized unit cycles on and off and wears out faster, while an undersized one runs flat out and fails to keep the house warm. Radiators often need replacing with larger ones because heat pumps run at lower flow temperatures than boilers.

Underfloor heating suits heat pumps because it works at low water temperatures around thirty five degrees. It is slow to respond, so households should keep a steady setting rather than switching it off during the day. Fitting it into an existing house means lifting floors, which makes it far costlier than in a new build.

Hot water cylinders for heat pumps are larger than normal and need a weekly high temperature cycle to kill legionella bacteria. That cycle uses an immersion element and briefly lowers efficiency. Cylinders should be insulated and located close to the taps to avoid long pipe runs that waste heat.

documents.name: energy-guide.pdf
pages: Hydropower dams store water behind a wall and release it through turbines, so output can be raised within seconds. Pumped storage plants run the turbines backwards at night to lift water uphill, acting as a giant battery for the grid. Biomass plants burn wood pellets or crop waste to raise steam. The fuel is only low carbon if the trees are replanted, and transporting bulky pellets over long distances erodes the saving. Tidal barrages trap the incoming tide in a basin and release it through turbines as the sea falls. They produce power on a precise timetable set by the moon, but damage the mudflats where wading birds feed. Nuclear reactors split uranium atoms to boil water. Spent fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and is stored in cooling ponds before burial in deep geological repositories.

Geothermal wells reach hot rock a few kilometres down and bring up steam or hot water. Iceland uses the heat for district heating, and plants need no fuel, but drilling can trigger small earthquakes. Green hydrogen is made by splitting water with renewable electricity in an electrolyser. It can fuel steelworks and long distance ships, yet roughly a third of the energy is lost in conversion. Waste to energy plants incinerate household rubbish to make electricity and heat. Filters capture the toxic gases, and the leftover ash is tested before being used in road building. Wave energy devices bob on the surface and pump hydraulic fluid through generators. Storms can destroy them, which is why most prototypes remain small and none yet compete on cost.
